entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Battle of Agrigentum, fought in 260 BCE, was a pivotal pitched battle between the Roman Republic and Carthage, marking the first large-scale military confrontation between the two powers. This conflict took place on the Sicilian coast, in the city of Agrigento, and would have far-reaching consequences for the Mediterranean region. The Roman Republic, led by the consuls Gaius Duilius and Gaius Sulpicius, emerged victorious, securing a crucial victory that would give them the upper hand in the First Punic War. The Carthaginians, led by the general Hanno, suffered heavy losses and were forced to retreat.

The Battle of Agrigentum was a significant turning point in the First Punic War, marking a shift in the balance of power between Rome and Carthage. The Roman victory would pave the way for further Roman expansion into the Mediterranean, ultimately leading to the downfall of Carthage. The battle also showcased the tactical genius of the Roman commander, Gaius Duilius, who would go on to become a legendary figure in Roman history.

In the aftermath of the battle, the Roman Republic would continue to push forward, expanding its territories and establishing itself as a dominant power in the Mediterranean. The Carthaginians, on the other hand, would be forced to regroup and re-strategize, but would continue to pose a threat to Roman interests in the region. The legacy of the Battle of Agrigentum can be seen in the subsequent Roman expansion into North Africa, which would eventually lead to the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE.

The Battle of Agrigentum remains an important chapter in the history of the Mediterranean, marking a critical moment in the struggle for power between Rome and Carthage. Its impact can still be felt today, with its legacy continuing to shape the politics and culture of the region.
